questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Value to What a Fourier Series Converges
questions.problem:
$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}, & x\in [-3,0] \\ -{x}^{2}, & x\in (0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=2.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{-}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is continuous at $x=2.$ 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
f(2)=-{2}^{2}=-4.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $F(x)=|x|$ defined on $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ).$ The Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{\pi }{2}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{\pi (2n-1)^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡((2n-1)x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.At $x=0,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡((2n-1)\cdot 0)={{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is 
{{field-2}}
at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(0)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}={{field-4}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our Fourier series as

$$
f(x)∼\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{4}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡((2n-1)x).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡((2n-1)\cdot 0)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(0)=0.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{4}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡((2n-1)\cdot 0) \\ 0 & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{4}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}}\cdot 1 \\ -\frac{\pi }{2} & =-\frac{4}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(2n-1)^{2}} & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Value to What a Fourier Series Converges
questions.problem:
$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2}, & x\in [-2,0) \\ 1, & x\in [0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=-2.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=-2.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(-2) & ={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x)=1 \\ {f}^{+}(-2) & ={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}f(x)={e}^{-2+2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(-2)+{f}^{+}(-2)}{2}=\frac{1+1}{2}=1.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Value of an Infinite Sum Using Fourier Series
questions.problem:
$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}-1, & x\in [-4,0] \\ 3, & x\in (0,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. The Fourier series of the $8$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{\pi (2n-1)}sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{4}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.At $x=-2,$ we have

$$
sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi \cdot (-2)}{4})={{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is 
{{field-2}}
at $x=-2,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(-2)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}={{field-4}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our Fourier series as

$$
f(x)∼1+\frac{8}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{4}).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=-2,$ we have

$$
sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi \cdot (-2)}{4})=sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}-n\pi )=(-1)^{n}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=-2,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(-2)=-1.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =1+\frac{8}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi \cdot (-2)}{4}) \\ -1 & =1+\frac{8}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot (-1)^{n} \\ -2 & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n-1} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n-1} & =-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. The Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼-1-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{16}{\pi (2n-1)}sin\,((2n-1)x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.At $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
sin\,((2n-1)\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}))={{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is 
{{field-2}}
at $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(-\frac{\pi }{2})={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}={{field-4}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our Fourier series as

$$
f(x)∼-1-\frac{16}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot sin\,((2n-1)x).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
sin\,((2n-1)\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}))=sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}-n\pi )=(-1)^{n}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(-\frac{\pi }{2})=3.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-1-\frac{16}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot sin\,((2n-1)\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ 3 & =-1-\frac{16}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot (-1)^{n} \\ 4 & =-\frac{16}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n-1} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n-1} & =-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
